header_line: Real PYQ Bank - Maths (Class XII level only, organized by chapter)
instructions: Every Class-XII-level Maths question from the real past papers you provided, organized by chapter. Degree-level content (complex analysis, PDEs, numerical methods, group theory - found in the 2015/2016/2018 ATC papers) has been excluded since it's beyond this exam's actual syllabus depth. Options are unticked - a simple, clear Answer and solution is directly below each question.

questions.q: The number of commutative binary operations on the set A = {1,2} is ______.
questions.info: This generalises: for an n-element set, total operations = n^(n^2), and commutative ones = n^(n(n+1)/2) (counting only the independent upper-triangle + diagonal cells).
questions.trick: Think of it as filling a table and just count degrees of freedom - commutativity halves the off-diagonal freedom, it doesn't need case-by-case checking.
questions.concept: A binary operation on a 2-element set is a 2x2 table (one output per ordered pair), each of the 4 cells fillable in 2 ways, giving 2^4=16 total operations.
calculation: Formula: a binary operation on A is a 2x2 table. Commutative means x*y = y*x for every pair.
A = {1,2} has 4 ordered pairs: (1,1), (2,2), (1,2), (2,1). So the table has 4 cells.
Commutative rule forces cell (1,2) to equal cell (2,1). So these two cells are not independent - they count as 1 free choice.
Free cells: (1,1), (2,2) and the pair {(1,2),(2,1)}. That is 3 free cells.
Each free cell can hold 1 or 2 (2 choices).
Count = 2 x 2 x 2 = 2^3.
Check with formula n^(n(n+1)/2) for n=2: n(n+1)/2 = 2*3/2 = 3, so 2^3 = 8.
Number of commutative operations = 8 (16 is the total without the commutative condition).
questions.formula: Total ops = n^(n^2); commutative ops = n^(n(n+1)/2)

questions.q: A binary operation '*' is defined on a set P. The operation is commutative if ______.
questions.info: Don't confuse commutative (order doesn't matter) with associative (grouping doesn't matter, (x*y)*z=x*(y*z)) - they're independent properties.
questions.trick: Pattern-match 'commutative' to 'swap the operands, same result' instantly - it's always x*y=y*x, never anything about grouping or identity elements.
questions.concept: This is a definition-recall question - no computation needed.
calculation: Definition: '*' is commutative if changing the order of the two numbers does not change the answer.
Option A: x*y = y*x. Order swapped, same answer. This is the commutative law.
Option B: (x*y)*z = x*(y*z). This is the associative law (grouping), not commutative.
Option C: (y o z)*x = (y*x) o (z*x). This is the distributive law, not commutative.
Option D: x*y = x. This says the answer is always the first number. It is not the commutative law.
So the commutative condition is x*y = y*x.

questions.q: Sets A and B have 3 and 4 elements respectively. The total number of possible relations from A to B is ______.
questions.info: This same idea extends to functions: the number of functions from A to B is |B|^|A|, a different (usually smaller) count than the number of relations.
questions.trick: Jump straight to 2^(|A|*|B|) for 'number of relations from A to B' - no need to enumerate the Cartesian product.
questions.concept: A relation from A to B is any subset of the Cartesian product A x B.
calculation: Formula: a relation from A to B is any subset of A x B. Number of relations = 2^(number of elements in A x B).
n(A) = 3 and n(B) = 4.
A set with 12 elements has 2^12 subsets.
So the number of relations from A to B = 2^12.
Do not pick 2^7 (that is 3+4, wrong: we multiply, not add).
questions.formula: Number of relations A to B = 2^(|A|*|B|)

questions.q: Which represents an empty set?
options: Set of vowels in the word SYNCH
Set of prime numbers less than 10
Set of consonants in the word GIRLS
Set of months of a year starting with letter A
questions.info: The empty set is still a perfectly valid set (not an error or undefined) - it's a subset of every set, including itself.
questions.trick: Scan each option's letters/numbers against the stated property quickly - the empty set option is the one where NOTHING matches.
questions.concept: Check each option's defining property for whether ANY element actually satisfies it.
calculation: Empty set means a set with no element at all. Test each option.
Option A: letters of SYNCH are S, Y, N, C, H. Vowels are A, E, I, O, U. None of these letters is a vowel. So the set is empty.
Option B: primes less than 10 are 2, 3, 5, 7. Not empty.
Option C: letters of GIRLS are G, I, R, L, S. Consonants are G, R, L, S. Not empty.
Option D: months starting with A are April and August. Not empty.
Only option A has no element, so it is the empty set. (Remember: Y is not a vowel in this question.)

questions.q: A = {24,36,48}, B = {12,18,24}, f: A -> B. Which function is neither one-one nor onto?
questions.info: A function failing one-one often ALSO fails onto when domain and codomain have equal size - if it repeats an output, it must necessarily miss another.
questions.trick: List each option's actual output values and check for (a) repeats = not one-one, (b) missing targets = not onto - two quick scans, no deep analysis needed.
questions.concept: One-one (injective) means no two inputs share an output; onto (surjective) means every element of B is hit.
calculation: Rules: one-one means no two inputs share the same output. Onto means every element of B = {12,18,24} is an output.
Option A: outputs 12, 18, 24 - all different and all of B. One-one and onto. Not the answer.
Option B (s): outputs 24, 12, 18 - all different and all of B. One-one and onto. Not the answer.
Option C (g): outputs 18, 24, 12 - all different and all of B. One-one and onto. Not the answer.
Option D (h): outputs 12, 18, 12. Inputs 24 and 48 both go to 12, so h is NOT one-one.
For h, the output set is {12, 18}. The element 24 of B is never reached, so h is NOT onto.
So h is neither one-one nor onto.

questions.q: If f(x)=sin(x), g(x)=3x, h(x)=x+4, what is h(g(f(x)))?
questions.info: This composition h(g(f(x))) is also written (h o g o f)(x) in function notation - same meaning, inside-out evaluation.
questions.trick: Replace one layer at a time, substituting the previous result as the new input - never try to combine all three functions in one step.
questions.concept: Work from the innermost function outward.
calculation: Rule: h(g(f(x))) means apply f first, then g, then h. Work from the inside.
First, f(x) = sin(x).
Next, g(f(x)) = g(sin x). Since g(x) = 3x, replace x by sin x: g(sin x) = 3 sin(x).
Last, h(g(f(x))) = h(3 sin x). Since h(x) = x + 4, replace x by 3 sin x: h(3 sin x) = 3 sin(x) + 4.
Check: sin(3x) in option A is wrong because 3 multiplies the sine, not the angle.
Result = 3*sin(x) + 4.

questions.q: Which relation is symmetric, but neither reflexive nor transitive?
questions.info: Contrast with 'parallel to' for lines, which IS an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, AND transitive) - a useful opposite example to keep in mind.
questions.trick: Test each property with a tiny concrete example (3 lines, 2 perpendicular pairs) rather than reasoning abstractly - concrete cases make reflexive/transitive failures obvious fast.
questions.concept: Check each option against the three properties: reflexive (related to itself), symmetric (if a~b then b~a), transitive (if a~b and b~c then a~c).
calculation: Reflexive: a is related to a. Symmetric: a~b gives b~a. Transitive: a~b and b~c gives a~c. Test each option.
Option A (congruent triangles): reflexive, symmetric and transitive. But we need NOT reflexive, so it fails.
Option B (similar triangles): reflexive, symmetric, transitive. Fails.
Option C (parallel lines): a line is parallel to itself (taken as reflexive), symmetric, transitive. Fails.
Option D (perpendicular lines): if L1 is perpendicular to L2 then L2 is perpendicular to L1. So it is symmetric.
A line is never perpendicular to itself. So it is NOT reflexive.
If L1 is perpendicular to L2 and L2 is perpendicular to L3, then L1 is parallel to L3, not perpendicular. So it is NOT transitive.
So perpendicularity is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive.

questions.info: Parentheses in set expressions work exactly like in arithmetic - always resolve the bracketed operation first before combining with the rest.
questions.trick: Physically cross out / circle shared elements for intersection, then just list everything for union - visual marking prevents double-counting.
questions.concept: Follow order of operations: compute the intersection first, then the union with C.
calculation: Order of work: first brackets (A intersect B), then union with C.
Common elements of A and B: only 54. So A intersect B = {54}.
Now take the union with C = {45,54,60}.
(A intersect B) union C = {54} union {45,54,60}.
Union means all elements together, writing 54 only once: {45,54,60}.
This is the same as C, because 54 was already in C.

questions.q: A={24,36,48}, B={12,18,24}, f:A->B. Which is an onto function?
questions.info: When |A|=|B| and a function is onto, it's automatically also one-one (and vice versa) - a bijection shortcut worth remembering for finite equal-size sets.
questions.trick: List out just the 3 output values from each option and check if they cover B exactly - skip checking one-one separately when |A|=|B|, it comes for free.
questions.concept: An onto (surjective) function must have every element of the codomain B appear as an output at least once.
calculation: Onto means every element of B = {12,18,24} appears as an output at least once.
Option A (h): outputs 12, 12, 24. The value 18 is missing. Not onto.
Option B (g): outputs 12, 12, 12. Values 18 and 24 are missing. Not onto.
Option C (f): outputs 12, 18, 24. All three elements of B are hit. Onto.
Option D (s): outputs 24, 12, 12. The value 18 is missing. Not onto.
Only f = {(24,12),(36,18),(48,24)} is onto. (It is also one-one since all outputs are different.)

questions.q: P={x: x=6n, n in N, n<=8}, Q={x: x=8n, n in N, n<=10}. What is P - Q?
questions.info: P-Q and Q-P are generally DIFFERENT sets (set difference is not symmetric) - don't assume they'd give the same answer.
questions.trick: List both sets fully first, then just cross out the shared elements from P - faster and less error-prone than trying to reason about the difference abstractly.
questions.concept: List out P fully: multiples of 6 from n=1 to 8: {6,12,18,24,30,36,42,48}.
calculation: Aim: P - Q means elements that are in P but not in Q.
Common elements of P and Q: 24 and 48 (both are in the lists above).
Remove 24 and 48 from P.
Check: 6 elements left, 8 - 2 = 6. Correct.

questions.q: Let L denote the set of all straight lines in a plane. Let a relation R be l R m if l is perpendicular to m for all l, m in L. Then R is:
questions.given: R on lines: l R m if l is perpendicular to m.
questions.concept: A relation is reflexive, symmetric, transitive by checking aRa, aRb implies bRa, aRb and bRc implies aRc.
calculation: Reflexive test: is l perpendicular to l? No, a line is never perpendicular to itself. So R is not reflexive.
Symmetric test: if l is perpendicular to m, then m is perpendicular to l. True. So R is symmetric.
Transitive test: l perpendicular to m and m perpendicular to n makes l parallel to n, not perpendicular.
So R is not transitive, hence not an equivalence relation.
Only symmetry holds. Matches option B.
questions.info: Parallelism of lines is an equivalence relation, while perpendicularity is only symmetric.
questions.trick: Perpendicular gives symmetric only; parallel gives all three properties.

questions.q: The domain of the function f: R to R defined by f(x) = sqrt(x^2 - 3x + 2) is:
questions.given: f(x) = sqrt(x^2 - 3x + 2); find the domain.
questions.concept: Square root is defined only when the expression inside is at least 0.
calculation: Condition: x^2 - 3x + 2 must be at least 0 for sqrt to be real.
Factorise: x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2).
Roots are x = 1 and x = 2.
A product (x-1)(x-2) is positive when x is below 1 or above 2, and zero at x = 1 and x = 2.
Include the end points since zero is allowed under the root.
Domain = (-inf,1] U [2,inf). Matches option A.
questions.info: For sqrt of a quadratic with positive leading coefficient, the domain lies outside the roots; for ln it would exclude the roots.
questions.trick: Upward parabola: at least 0 means outside the roots, with brackets closed for sqrt.

questions.q: Let R be the set of real numbers and * be the binary operation defined on R as a * b = a + b - ab for all a, b in R. Then, the identity element with respect to the binary operation * is:
questions.given: a * b = a + b - ab on R; find the identity e.
questions.concept: Identity e satisfies a * e = a for every a.
calculation: Condition: a * e = a for all a in R.
a * e = a + e - ae.
Set a + e - ae = a.
Cancel a from both sides: e - ae = 0.
Factor: e(1 - a) = 0.
This holds for all a only when e = 0.
Check: a * 0 = a + 0 - 0 = a. Identity is 0. Matches option D.
questions.info: Here a * b = a + b - ab equals 1 - (1-a)(1-b), so the inverse of a is a/(a-1) for a not equal to 1.
questions.trick: Put b = 0 in the rule: a + 0 - 0 = a, so 0 works as identity.

questions.q: What is the conjugate of the complex number z = 3i + 7?
questions.info: A useful identity: z * (conjugate of z) = |z|^2 (always a real, non-negative number) - this is why conjugates are used to simplify division by complex numbers.
questions.trick: Just flip the sign in front of i - no other part of the number changes, this is a one-step operation.
questions.concept: The complex conjugate of a+bi is a-bi - just flip the sign of the imaginary part.
calculation: Formula: conjugate of a + bi is a - bi. Only the sign of the imaginary part changes.
Write z in standard form: z = 3i + 7 = 7 + 3i. So a = 7 and b = 3.
Change the sign of the imaginary part: 7 - 3i.
Write it like the options: 7 - 3i = -3i + 7.
This matches option B.

questions.q: If (3i-2)^2 + (5i+6)^2 = a + ib, what is a+b?
questions.info: Substituting i^2=-1 is the single most important step in any complex-number expansion - always do the full algebraic expansion first, then substitute i^2=-1 last to avoid sign errors.
questions.trick: Expand fully first treating i like a normal variable, THEN substitute i^2=-1 at the very end - trying to substitute mid-expansion causes most sign mistakes.
questions.concept: Expand each square separately using (x+y)^2=x^2+2xy+y^2.
calculation: Formula: (x + y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2, and i^2 = -1.
Compare with a + ib: a = 6 and b = 48.

questions.q: What is the square root of z = 7 - 24i?
questions.info: Every non-zero complex number has exactly 2 square roots, always negatives of each other - just like real numbers have ± square roots.
questions.trick: If the options are given, square each candidate back and check which one reproduces 7-24i - often much faster than solving the x,y system from scratch.
questions.concept: Assume sqrt(z) = x+yi for real x,y, so (x+yi)^2 = 7-24i.
calculation: Let sqrt(7 - 24i) = x + yi with x and y real. Squaring: (x + yi)^2 = x^2 - y^2 + 2xyi.
Equate real and imaginary parts: x^2 - y^2 = 7 (equation 1) and 2xy = -24, so xy = -12 (equation 2).
Modulus: x^2 + y^2 = |z| = sqrt(7^2 + 24^2) = sqrt(49 + 576) = sqrt(625) = 25 (equation 3).
Add equations 1 and 3: 2x^2 = 32, so x^2 = 16 and x = 4 or -4.
Subtract equation 1 from 3: 2y^2 = 18, so y^2 = 9 and y = 3 or -3.
From xy = -12, x and y have opposite signs. So (x, y) = (4, -3) or (-4, 3).
So the square roots are 4 - 3i and -4 + 3i, i.e. +/-(4 - 3i).

questions.q: What is the multiplicative inverse of z = 12 - 5i?
questions.info: 12,5,13 is a Pythagorean triple (12^2+5^2=13^2=169) - recognising this instantly gives |z|=13 without needing to compute sqrt(169) by hand.
questions.trick: Multiply by the conjugate over the modulus-squared immediately - this is the ONLY method needed for inverting any complex number, no other approach is faster.
questions.concept: Multiplicative inverse of z is 1/z, found by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate: 1/z = conjugate(z)/|z|^2.
calculation: Formula: 1/z = conjugate(z) / |z|^2, where |z|^2 = a^2 + b^2 for z = a + bi.
Here z = 12 - 5i, so a = 12 and b = -5.
Conjugate of z = 12 + 5i.
Split into real and imaginary parts: 1/z = 12/169 + (5/169)i.

questions.q: If alpha, beta are zeroes of p(x) = x^2 - 25x + 150, what is 1/alpha + 1/beta?
questions.info: This sum/product shortcut generalises to ANY symmetric combination of roots (like sum of squares, or 1/root1+1/root2) without ever solving the quadratic explicitly.
questions.trick: Reach for sum=-b/a, product=c/a immediately instead of the quadratic formula - for integer-root quadratics this is almost always faster.
questions.concept: For x^2-bx+c, sum of roots = b (here 25) and product of roots = c (here 150) - read directly off the coefficients.
calculation: Roots of x^2 - 25x + 150: find two numbers with sum 25 and product 150.
Try 10 and 15: 10 + 15 = 25 and 10 * 15 = 150. Good, so alpha and beta are 10 and 15.
Formula: 1/alpha + 1/beta = (alpha + beta) / (alpha * beta).
Substitute: = 25 / 150.
Divide top and bottom by 25: 25/150 = 1/6.
So 1/alpha + 1/beta = 1/6.
questions.formula: For x^2-bx+c: sum of roots=b, product of roots=c

questions.q: What are the roots of 8x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0?
questions.info: A perfect-square discriminant is a strong hint that the quadratic factors nicely with rational roots - always check this before committing to the full formula.
questions.trick: Check if the discriminant is a perfect square FIRST - if so, factor directly instead of grinding through the quadratic formula, it's faster and less error-prone.
questions.concept: Try factoring first since the discriminant might be a perfect square: discriminant = (-2)^2-4(8)(-3) = 4+96=100=10^2 (a perfect square - nice roots expected).
calculation: Formula: for ax^2 + bx + c = 0, x = [-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)] / (2a). Here a = 8, b = -2, c = -3.
Plus sign: x = 12/16 = 3/4.
Minus sign: x = -8/16 = -1/2.
Check by factoring: (4x - 3)(2x + 1) = 8x^2 + 4x - 6x - 3 = 8x^2 - 2x - 3. Correct.
Roots are 3/4 and -1/2.

questions.q: If one root of the quadratic equation x^2 - 8tx - 25 = 0 is 3 + 4t, then the other root must be:
questions.given: Quadratic x^2 - 8t*x - 25 = 0 with one root 3 + 4t; find the other root.
questions.concept: Sum of roots = -b/a = 8t, so other root = 8t - (given root).
calculation: Formula: for x^2 + bx + c = 0, sum of roots = -b.
Here b = -8t, so the sum of the roots = 8t.
One root is 3 + 4t.
Other root = 8t - (3 + 4t).
This is option D.
questions.info: Using the product of roots instead gives (3 + 4t)(-3 + 4t) = 16t^2 - 9 = -25, which holds only for t^2 = -1, so the stem is consistent only for such t; the sum-of-roots method gives the intended answer.
questions.trick: Always use the sum of roots when the middle coefficient is given; it needs just one subtraction.

questions.q: In a triangle ABC, sec(A) * [sin(B)cos(C) + cos(B)sin(C)] equals:
questions.info: This 'angles of a triangle sum to 180' substitution is a very common trick in triangle-trigonometry MCQs - always check if an expression simplifies once you replace B+C with 180-A.
questions.trick: Spot the sin(B+C) pattern immediately from the bracket's shape - don't expand or plug in numbers, just apply the compound-angle identity directly.
questions.concept: Recognise the bracket as the sine addition formula: sin(B)cos(C)+cos(B)sin(C) = sin(B+C).
calculation: Formula: sin(B + C) = sin B cos C + cos B sin C. The bracket is exactly this.
So the expression = sec A * sin(B + C).
In a triangle, A + B + C = 180 degrees, so B + C = 180 - A.
sin(180 - A) = sin A (sine stays positive in the second quadrant).
Expression = sec A * sin A.
Use sec A = 1/cos A: (1/cos A) * sin A = sin A / cos A.
sin A / cos A = tan A.

questions.q: The value of tan(315 degrees) is the same as the value of:
questions.info: Memorise the quadrant sign rule 'All Students Take Calculus' (ASTC): All positive in Q1, Sin positive in Q2, Tan positive in Q3, Cos positive in Q4 - everything else is negative.
questions.trick: Reduce any angle to its nearest multiple of 90 and compare against the reference angle (like 45 here) with the correct quadrant sign - no need to compute decimal values.
questions.concept: 315 degrees = 360-45, placing it in the 4th quadrant where tan is negative: tan(315) = -tan(45) = -1.
calculation: Aim: find tan 315 first, then match with the options.
315 = 360 - 45, so the angle is in the 4th quadrant where tan is negative.
Option A: tan 135 = tan(180 - 45) = -tan 45 = -1 (2nd quadrant, tan negative). Matches.
Option B: sin 90 = 1. Not equal to -1.
Option C: sin 180 = 0. Not equal to -1.
Option D: cos 0 = 1. Not equal to -1.
Only tan 135 equals -1.

questions.q: Simplify cos(x)/(1-sin(x)) using trigonometric identities:
questions.info: This '(1 ± sin x)' or '(1 ± cos x)' denominator pattern almost always clears nicely via the Pythagorean identity sin^2+cos^2=1 once you multiply by the conjugate.
questions.trick: Whenever you see (1-sin x) or (1+cos x) alone in a denominator, immediately multiply top and bottom by its 'partner' (1+sin x) or (1-cos x) - it always converts to a clean cos^2 or sin^2 term.
questions.concept: Multiply top and bottom by (1+sin x), a classic 'rationalising' move for this is-1-sin(x) pattern.
calculation: Aim: remove sin x from the denominator. Multiply top and bottom by (1 + sin x).
cos x / (1 - sin x) = cos x (1 + sin x) / [(1 - sin x)(1 + sin x)].
Denominator: (1 - sin x)(1 + sin x) = 1 - sin^2 x (since (a-b)(a+b) = a^2 - b^2).
Use sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1, so 1 - sin^2 x = cos^2 x.
Expression = cos x (1 + sin x) / cos^2 x.
Cancel one cos x: = (1 + sin x) / cos x.
Split: = 1/cos x + sin x/cos x = sec x + tan x.
Check: sec x - tan x = (1 - sin x)/cos x is the reciprocal form, so it is wrong. Result = sec x + tan x, option C.

questions.q: The value of cos(45+theta) - sin(45+theta) is:
questions.info: Expressions like cos(A+B)-sin(A+B) (or the sum version) often collapse to a single sin or cos term scaled by sqrt2 - this is the basis of the 'R-method' used to combine a*sinx+b*cosx into one wave.
questions.trick: When you see 45 degrees paired with another angle, substitute sin45=cos45=1/sqrt2 immediately - it usually causes massive cancellation within 2-3 lines.
questions.concept: Expand both using the compound-angle formulas: cos(45+theta)=cos45*cos(theta)-sin45*sin(theta), and sin(45+theta)=sin45*cos(theta)+cos45*sin(theta).
calculation: Formula: cos(A+B) = cosA cosB - sinA sinB and sin(A+B) = sinA cosB + cosA sinB. Take A = 45 and B = theta.
We know cos45 = sin45 = 1/sqrt2.
cos(45+theta) = (1/sqrt2)cos(theta) - (1/sqrt2)sin(theta) = [cos(theta) - sin(theta)]/sqrt2.
sin(45+theta) = (1/sqrt2)cos(theta) + (1/sqrt2)sin(theta) = [cos(theta) + sin(theta)]/sqrt2.
Subtract: [cos(theta) - sin(theta) - cos(theta) - sin(theta)]/sqrt2. Careful: the minus sign changes both terms of the second bracket.
cos(theta) cancels with - cos(theta). Left with -2sin(theta)/sqrt2.
Write 2/sqrt2 = sqrt2 (multiply top and bottom by sqrt2). So the answer is -sqrt2 sin(theta), option D.

questions.q: Find the degree measure of 6 radians.
questions.info: 6 radians is just under 2*pi (≈6.283), so it represents just under one full circle (360 degrees) - that's a fast sanity check that the answer should be close to but just under 360.
questions.trick: For a quick sanity check before computing exactly: 1 radian ≈ 57.3 degrees, so 6 radians ≈ 6*57.3 ≈ 344 degrees - lets you eliminate obviously-wrong options instantly.
questions.concept: Convert using: degrees = radians * (180/pi).
calculation: Formula: degrees = radians x (180/pi). Here radians = 6.
Degrees = 6 x 180/pi = 1080/pi.
Convert the decimal part to minutes: 0.6364 x 60 = 38.18 minutes. So 38 minutes and 0.18 minute left.
Convert 0.18 minute to seconds: 0.18 x 60 = 10.8, about 11 seconds.
So 6 radians = 343 deg 38' 11" approx (matches option A; the others have 337, 334, 327 degrees which are too small).

questions.q: Determine the value of sin(21*pi/2) and cos(-1740 degrees).
questions.info: Cosine is an EVEN function (cos(-x)=cos(x)) while sine is ODD (sin(-x)=-sin(x)) - always apply this sign rule first before reducing a negative angle.
questions.trick: Always reduce large angles modulo 360 degrees (or 2*pi radians) FIRST before doing anything else - it turns an intimidating-looking angle into one of the standard 0/30/45/60/90-based values.
questions.concept: For sin(21*pi/2): since sine repeats every 2*pi, subtract multiples of 2*pi (=4*pi/2) until the angle is in a familiar range. 21*pi/2 - 10*pi (=20*pi/2) = pi/2.
calculation: Part 1: sin(21pi/2). Sine repeats every 2pi, so remove full turns of 2pi = 4pi/2.
21pi/2 = 20pi/2 + pi/2 = 10pi + pi/2. And 10pi is 5 full turns of 2pi.
So sin(21pi/2) = sin(pi/2) = 1.
Part 2: cos(-1740 deg). Cosine is even: cos(-x) = cos(x). So cos(-1740) = cos(1740).
Remove full turns of 360: 4 x 360 = 1440, and 1740 - 1440 = 300. So cos(1740) = cos(300).
300 = 360 - 60, and cos(360 - 60) = cos(60) = 1/2 (cos is positive in 4th quadrant).
So the pair is (1, 1/2), option D. First value 1 already rules out the other three options.

questions.q: If arcs of equal length in two circles subtend angles 70 and 120 degrees at the centre, determine the ratio of their radii.
questions.info: Notice the ratio is INVERTED compared to what you might first guess - the circle with the SMALLER angle needs the LARGER radius to produce the same arc length.
questions.trick: For 'equal arc length, find ratio of radii' questions, just flip the ratio of the given angles - r1:r2 = theta_2:theta_1, not theta_1:theta_2.
questions.concept: Arc length formula: arc = radius * angle (angle in radians, but the ratio works the same with degrees since it cancels out).
calculation: Formula: arc length = radius x angle, so l = r x theta (same angle unit for both circles).
Let the radii be r1 and r2 with angles 70 and 120 degrees. Arcs are equal.
So r1 x 70 = r2 x 120.
Divide both sides by r2 and by 70: r1/r2 = 120/70.
Multiply top and bottom by 2: 12/7 = 24/14.
So r1 : r2 = 24 : 14, option A. (Degrees can be used directly because the degree-to-radian factor cancels in the ratio.)

questions.q: For the fourth quadrant (point P(a,b), unit circle), which option correctly describes it?
questions.info: This directly mirrors the ASTC rule: in Q4 only cosine (and its reciprocal secant) are positive; sine, tan, cosec, cot are all negative there.
questions.trick: Memorise quadrant ranges as fractions of a full circle: Q1=(0,1/4), Q2=(1/4,1/2), Q3=(1/2,3/4), Q4=(3/4,1) of 2pi - makes matching angle ranges to quadrants instant.
questions.concept: The four quadrants on a standard unit circle, going counterclockwise from 0, are: Q1 (0 to pi/2), Q2 (pi/2 to pi), Q3 (pi to 3pi/2), Q4 (3pi/2 to 2pi).
calculation: On the unit circle, point P(a,b) has a = cos(x) and b = sin(x). Angle x is measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.
Q1: 0 to pi/2, a positive, b positive.
Q2: pi/2 to pi, a negative, b positive.
Q3: pi to 3pi/2, a negative, b negative.
Q4: 3pi/2 to 2pi, a positive, b negative.
Check options: option B has range 0 to pi/2 which is Q1 (b would be positive), so it fails. 3rd has pi/2 to pi which is Q2 (a negative), fails. 4th has pi to 3pi/2 which is Q3 (both negative), fails.
Only option A, 3pi/2 less than x less than 2pi with a positive and b negative, is Q4.

questions.q: If cos(x)=5/13 and x is in the third quadrant, find the other five trig functions.
questions.info: A common trap: knowing ONE ratio's sign isn't enough - you must apply the quadrant's sign rule to EVERY derived ratio separately, not assume they all flip the same way.
questions.trick: Draw a quick mental (or actual) CAST diagram and mark + or - for sin/cos/tan in each quadrant before computing anything - prevents sign mistakes under exam time pressure.
questions.concept: In the third quadrant, both sine and cosine are negative (only tan and cot are positive there).
calculation: Use the given value cos(x) = 5/13. Use sin^2(x) + cos^2(x) = 1.
sin(x) = plus or minus 12/13. All the options show sin negative, so take sin(x) = -12/13.
Check options: options A and D have sin positive, so they fail. Option B has cosec = -13/13 which is wrong (should be -13/12). Only option C matches all five values.
Note: the question says third quadrant, but cos = 5/13 is positive there (a typo in the question). Just match the sign pattern of the options in the exam.

questions.q: Let theta = arcsin(sin(-600 degrees)), then the value of theta is:
questions.given: theta = arcsin(sin(-600 degrees)).
questions.concept: arcsin returns an angle in [-90 degrees, 90 degrees], so reduce sin(-600 degrees) to an angle in that range.
calculation: Use sin(-x) = -sin x: sin(-600 degrees) = -sin(600 degrees).
600 degrees = 360 degrees + 240 degrees, so sin(600 degrees) = sin(240 degrees).
sin(240 degrees) = sin(180 degrees + 60 degrees) = -sin(60 degrees) = -sqrt(3)/2.
So sin(-600 degrees) = -(-sqrt(3)/2) = sqrt(3)/2.
theta = arcsin(sqrt(3)/2). Principal value must lie in -90 degrees to 90 degrees.
arcsin(sqrt(3)/2) = 60 degrees = pi/3. Matches option A.
questions.info: arcsin(sin x) equals x only when x lies in [-pi/2, pi/2]; otherwise shift x into that interval first.
questions.trick: Reduce the angle by 360 degrees multiples, then fold into -90 to 90 degrees range.

questions.q: Minimum value of 27^(cos x) * 81^(sin x)
questions.given: Expression 27^(cos x) * 81^(sin x); find its minimum value.
questions.concept: Write with base 3, then use the range of a cos x + b sin x: from -sqrt(a^2+b^2) to sqrt(a^2+b^2).
calculation: Expression = 3^(3 cos x) * 3^(4 sin x) = 3^(3 cos x + 4 sin x).
Range of 3 cos x + 4 sin x is from -sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) to +sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = from -5 to 5.
Since 3^t is increasing in t, the minimum occurs at t = -5.
Minimum value = 3^(-5) = 1/3^5.
This matches option C.
questions.info: The maximum of the same expression is 3^5 = 243, at the same x where 3 cos x + 4 sin x = 5.
questions.trick: Convert to one base, then use the 3-4-5 triple: the exponent ranges over [-5, 5]. Minimum is the base to the power -5.
questions.formula: min of a cos x + b sin x = -sqrt(a^2 + b^2)

questions.q: In a triangle ABC, if AB = 5, BC = 3 and CA = 4, then the value of sin(A/2) + tan(A/2) is:
questions.given: Sides 3, 4, 5, so the triangle is right-angled at C; angle A is opposite BC = 3.
questions.concept: Half-angle formulas: sin(A/2) = sqrt((1 - cos A)/2), tan(A/2) = sin A/(1 + cos A).
calculation: Since 3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2, the triangle is right-angled at C with hypotenuse AB = 5.
sin A = BC/AB = 3/5 and cos A = AC/AB = 4/5.
This matches option C.
questions.info: For half angles in any triangle, tan(A/2) = r/(s - a). Here s = 6, a = 3, r = 1, so tan(A/2) = 1/3 as well.
questions.trick: Spot the 3-4-5 triangle first: all trig ratios become instant fractions.

questions.q: The greatest value of 5 sin^2 x + 7 cos^2 x - 4 sin x cos x will be:
questions.given: Expression E = 5 sin^2 x + 7 cos^2 x - 4 sin x cos x.
questions.concept: Convert to double angle: sin^2 x = (1 - cos 2x)/2, cos^2 x = (1 + cos 2x)/2, 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x.
calculation: Write 5 sin^2 x + 7 cos^2 x = 6 (sin^2 x + cos^2 x) + (cos^2 x - sin^2 x) = 6 + cos 2x.
Also 4 sin x cos x = 2 * (2 sin x cos x) = 2 sin 2x.
So E = 6 + cos 2x - 2 sin 2x.
Max of cos 2x - 2 sin 2x is sqrt(1^2 + (-2)^2) = sqrt(5).
Greatest value of E = 6 + sqrt(5).
This is option B.
questions.info: The least value is 6 - sqrt(5). The expression always lies between 6 - sqrt(5) and 6 + sqrt(5).
questions.trick: Reduce to constant + a*cos(2x) + b*sin(2x); the extreme is constant plus or minus sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
questions.formula: max of p*cos(t) + q*sin(t) is sqrt(p^2 + q^2)

questions.q: The value of 2 arctan(2/3) + arccos(12/13) is:
questions.given: Evaluate 2*arctan(2/3) + arccos(12/13).
questions.concept: 2*arctan(x) = arctan(2x/(1 - x^2)) for |x| less than 1; arccos(12/13) = arctan(5/12).
calculation: Formula: 2*arctan(x) = arctan(2x/(1 - x^2)).
For arccos(12/13): cos = 12/13 gives sin = 5/13, so tan = 5/12 and arccos(12/13) = arctan(5/12).
Sum = arctan(12/5) + arctan(5/12).
arctan(a) + arctan(1/a) = pi/2 for a greater than 0, so the sum = pi/2.
This is option A.
questions.info: 2*arctan(x) can also be written as arcsin(2x/(1 + x^2)) or arccos((1 - x^2)/(1 + x^2)).
questions.trick: Spot the pair arctan(a) + arctan(1/a) = pi/2; it turns most such sums into pi/2 instantly.

questions.q: The distance of the highest point on the graph of the function y = 12 cos x - 5 sin x from the x-axis is:
questions.given: Function y = 12 cos x - 5 sin x; find the height of its highest point above the x-axis.
questions.concept: a cos x + b sin x has maximum value sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
calculation: Formula: the maximum of a cos x + b sin x is sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
Here a = 12 and b = -5.
Maximum y = sqrt(169) = 13.
The highest point lies 13 units above the x-axis, so the distance is 13.
This is option A.
questions.info: Write it as R cos(x + phi) with R = 13; the graph oscillates between -13 and 13.
questions.trick: Spot the Pythagorean triples 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and 7-24-25; they give the amplitude immediately.
questions.formula: max of (a cos x + b sin x) = sqrt(a^2 + b^2)

questions.q: (sin15A + sin5A)/(cos15A + cos5A) = ______.
questions.given: (sin15A + sin5A)/(cos15A + cos5A).
questions.concept: Sum-to-product formulas for sine and cosine.
calculation: Formula: sinC + sinD = 2sin((C+D)/2)cos((C-D)/2).
Formula: cosC + cosD = 2cos((C+D)/2)cos((C-D)/2).
Here (C+D)/2 = 10A and (C-D)/2 = 5A.
Numerator = 2sin10A cos5A.
Denominator = 2cos10A cos5A.
Cancel 2cos5A: ratio = sin10A/cos10A = tan10A. Matches option C.
questions.info: In general (sinC + sinD)/(cosC + cosD) = tan((C+D)/2).
questions.trick: For a sum of sines over a sum of cosines, the answer is tan of the average angle.

questions.concept: Addition formula for inverse tangent when xy is less than 1.
calculation: Formula: tan^-1 x + tan^-1 y = tan^-1((x + y)/(1 - xy)), valid when xy is less than 1.
x = 1/3, y = 1/7, so xy = 1/21 (less than 1, formula applies).
Result = tan^-1(1/2). Matches option A.
questions.info: If xy is greater than 1, add pi to the result; for xy = 1 the sum is pi/2.
questions.trick: Add the fractions and divide by (1 - product); the 21s cancel, leaving 10/20.

questions.q: What is the range of the function f(x) = 1 + 3cos2x?
questions.given: f(x) = 1 + 3cos2x.
questions.concept: cos of anything lies in [-1,1]; scale and shift.
calculation: Formula: -1 at most cos2x at most 1 for all x.
Multiply by 3: -3 at most 3cos2x at most 3.
Add 1: -2 at most 1 + 3cos2x at most 4.
So f(x) takes every value from -2 to 4.
Range = [-2, 4]. Matches option B.
questions.info: Range of a + b*cos(cx) is [a - |b|, a + |b|]; the coefficient c only changes the period.
questions.trick: Take a minus and plus |b|: 1 - 3 = -2 and 1 + 3 = 4.

questions.q: What is the sum to infinity of the GP: 2, 0.2, 0.02, 0.002, ...?
questions.info: 2.2222... as a fraction is exactly 20/9 - recognising a repeating decimal as a GP sum is a neat way to convert decimals to fractions quickly.
questions.trick: Always check |r|<1 before using the infinite-sum formula - if |r|>=1, the series diverges and has no finite sum (a common conceptual trap in MCQs).
questions.concept: Identify first term a=2 and common ratio r (each term is 1/10 of the previous): r=0.1.
calculation: Common ratio r = second term / first term = 0.2/2 = 0.1.
Since |r| = 0.1 is less than 1, the sum to infinity exists. Formula: S = a/(1 - r).
Multiply top and bottom by 10: 2/0.9 = 20/9.
Divide 20 by 9: 20/9 = 2.2222... (repeating), option A.
Check the others: 3.00 is too big, and 200/99 = 2.0202... is not equal to 20/9.

questions.q: Find three consecutive terms in an AP whose sum and product are 48 and 3840 respectively.
questions.info: This 'symmetric representation' trick (a-d, a, a+d) works for any 3-term AP problem and instantly removes one variable from the sum equation.
questions.trick: Whenever a problem gives consecutive AP/GP terms plus their sum, always set them up symmetrically around a middle term - the sum equation then solves in one line.
questions.concept: Represent the 3 consecutive AP terms symmetrically as (a-d), a, (a+d) - this makes the sum simplify nicely.
calculation: Let the three terms be (a - d), a, (a + d). This makes d cancel in the sum.
Product: (a - d) x a x (a + d) = a(a^2 - d^2) = 3840.
Put a = 16: 16(256 - d^2) = 3840. Divide both sides by 16: 256 - d^2 = 240.
So d^2 = 256 - 240 = 16, giving d = 4 (d = -4 gives the same terms in reverse).
Check: sum = 12 + 16 + 20 = 48. Product = 12 x 16 x 20 = 192 x 20 = 3840. So the answer is 12, 16, 20, option D.

questions.q: If the nth term of a sequence is a_n = 5n + 3, what is its 21st term?
questions.info: Not every 'sequence' question is really about arithmetic progressions - when the nth-term formula is given directly, it's pure substitution, regardless of what chapter the question sits in.
questions.trick: Always check if the nth term formula is given explicitly before reaching for AP sum/term formulas - if it is, just plug in the number directly, it's faster.
questions.concept: Direct substitution - no need for any AP formula since a_n is already given explicitly.
calculation: The nth term is given: a_n = 5n + 3. No AP formula needed, just put n = 21.

questions.q: The 9th term of an AP is 0. Which term is double its 19th term?
questions.info: Expressing everything in terms of 'd' (letting 'a' cancel out via the given condition) is the standard technique whenever a problem gives you one term equal to zero or a fixed value.
questions.trick: When a term is stated to equal 0, immediately substitute to eliminate 'a' in terms of 'd' - this turns a 2-variable problem into a 1-variable one.
questions.concept: AP's nth term: a_n = a+(n-1)d. The 9th term being 0 means a+8d=0, so a=-8d.
calculation: Formula: a_n = a + (n - 1)d.
9th term is 0: a + 8d = 0, so a = -8d.
19th term = a + 18d = -8d + 18d = 10d.
Double the 19th term = 2 x 10d = 20d.
Let the nth term equal 20d: a + (n - 1)d = 20d. Put a = -8d: -8d + (n - 1)d = 20d.
Divide both sides by d (d is not 0, else all terms are 0): -8 + (n - 1) = 20.
n - 1 = 28, so n = 29. The 29th term is double the 19th term, option B.

questions.q: If a_n = 6n - 1 is the general term of an AP, what is the sum of the first 10 terms?
questions.info: This 'average of first and last, times count' shortcut is exactly how Gauss famously summed 1 to 100 as a child - it works for ANY AP, not just ones starting at 1.
questions.trick: You never need the full S_n = n/2[2a+(n-1)d] formula if you can quickly find both the first and last (nth) term - just average them and multiply by n.
questions.concept: First term: a_1 = 6(1)-1 = 5. Tenth term: a_10 = 6(10)-1 = 59.
calculation: General term a_n = 6n - 1. Find first and last terms of the 10 terms.
First term: a_1 = 6(1) - 1 = 5.
Formula: S_n = (n/2)(first term + last term).
5 x 64 = 320, option D. (Note 59 is only the last term, not the sum.)

questions.q: The sum of the series 1 + 2(a^2+1) + 3(a^2+1)^2 + 4(a^2+1)^3 + ... will be:
questions.given: Series 1 + 2r + 3r^2 + 4r^3 + ... with r = a^2 + 1, taken as infinite.
questions.concept: 1 + 2r + 3r^2 + ... = 1/(1 - r)^2 for |r| less than 1 (arithmetico-geometric series).
calculation: Formula: 1 + 2r + 3r^2 + 4r^3 + ... = 1/(1 - r)^2 (infinite series, |r| less than 1).
Here r = a^2 + 1.
Sum = 1/a^4.
This is option A.
questions.info: The series is the derivative of the GP: d/dr (1 + r + r^2 + ...) = d/dr (1/(1 - r)) = 1/(1 - r)^2.
questions.trick: Coefficients 1, 2, 3, 4 with powers of r means the answer is always 1/(1 - r)^2.

questions.q: Set P has 4 elements and set Q has 5 elements. The number of injections from P to Q is:
questions.info: Injections from a size-p set to a size-q set only exist when q>=p - if Q had fewer elements than P, the answer would be 0 (not enough distinct targets).
questions.trick: Whenever you see 'number of injections/one-one functions from A to B', translate it immediately to nPr with n=|B|, r=|A| - it's always a permutation, never a combination.
questions.concept: An injection (one-one function) means each of P's 4 elements maps to a DIFFERENT element of Q - equivalent to arranging 4 of Q's 5 elements in order.
calculation: Injection means every element of P goes to a different element of Q.
First element of P has 5 choices in Q. Second has 4 (one is used). Third has 3. Fourth has 2.
This is a permutation of 5 things taken 4 at a time. Formula: nPr = n!/(n - r)!.
So the number of injections = 120, option D.

questions.q: How many words can be formed from the letters of COMPUTER with all vowels together?
questions.info: This 'glue the required-together letters into one block' technique is the standard method for ANY 'letters must stay together' word-arrangement question - always multiply by the internal arrangements of the glued block at the end.
questions.trick: Count the block as ONE unit first, get that count, THEN multiply by the internal permutations of what's inside the block - doing it in the other order is a common source of errors.
questions.concept: COMPUTER has 8 distinct letters: vowels O,U,E (3 of them) and consonants C,M,P,T,R (5 of them).
calculation: COMPUTER has 8 different letters. Vowels: O, U, E (3). Consonants: C, M, P, T, R (5).
Vowels must be together, so tie them into one block.
Now we arrange 5 consonants + 1 block = 6 units. Ways = 6! = 720.
Inside the block, the 3 vowels can swap among themselves in 3! = 6 ways.
Total = 6! x 3! (multiply because both happen together).
720 x 6 = 4320, option D. (720 alone is only the outer arrangement, so it is wrong.)

questions.q: A quiz team of 5 is chosen from 6 boys and 5 girls, with at most 2 girls. In how many ways?
questions.info: 'At most' problems need you to ADD UP multiple cases (0,1,2,... up to the limit); 'at least' problems are usually faster solved via the COMPLEMENT (total minus the cases that fail) - recognising which phrasing you have saves real time.
questions.trick: For small limits like 'at most 2', just directly sum the 3 cases - it's only 3 calculations. Save the complement trick for when the limit is large (e.g. 'at most 8 out of 10').
questions.concept: 'At most 2 girls' means we need to add up 3 separate cases: 0 girls, 1 girl, or 2 girls (each paired with enough boys to make 5 total).
calculation: Team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls. At most 2 girls means 0, 1 or 2 girls. Add the three cases.
Formula: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!).
0 girls, 5 boys: 5C0 x 6C5 = 1 x 6 = 6.
Total = 6 + 75 + 200 = 281, option B.

questions.q: 60 words (with/without meaning) can be made from all letters of AGAIN. Figure out the 49th word in dictionary/wordbook order.
questions.info: This 'dictionary order / rank of a word' technique is a classic Permutations topic - the key is counting how many words EACH possible starting letter contributes, in alphabetical order, before reaching the target position.
questions.trick: Build a running total position-by-position (24, then 36, then 48, then 60) rather than trying to compute the rank directly - as soon as the running total passes your target number (49), you know which starting letter's block you're in.
questions.concept: AGAIN has 5 letters: A,A,G,I,N (A repeats twice), giving 5!/2! = 60 total arrangements - matching the '60' stated in the question.
calculation: Letters of AGAIN in alphabetical order: A, A, G, I, N. Total words = 5!/2! = 60.
Words starting with A: remaining letters A, G, I, N are all different, so 4! = 24 words. These are words 1 to 24.
Words starting with G: remaining A, A, I, N. Ways = 4!/2! = 12. These are words 25 to 36.
Words starting with I: remaining A, A, G, N. Ways = 4!/2! = 12. These are words 37 to 48.
So 24 + 12 + 12 = 48 words come before any word starting with N.
The 49th word is the first word starting with N. Arrange the remaining A, A, G, I in alphabetical order: A, A, G, I.
So the 49th word = N + AAGI = NAAGI, option D.

questions.q: What is the number of permutations of n objects taken all at a time, with p1 of one kind, p2 of another, ..., pk of a kth kind (rest all different)?
questions.info: This exact formula is what you'd use to count arrangements of a word like MISSISSIPPI, where letters repeat multiple times - divide the total factorial by each repeated letter's own factorial.
questions.trick: Spot this formula pattern instantly: whenever a word/problem has repeated identical items, the answer is always (total)! divided by (count of each repeated type)! for every repeated type.
questions.concept: This is a definition/formula-recall question, not a calculation.
calculation: Standard result: if n objects have p1 identical of one kind, p2 identical of another, ..., pk of a kth kind, the arrangements of all n are n!/(p1! x p2! x ... x pk!).
Why: n! counts identical objects as different. Each group of p identical objects is over-counted p! times, so divide by p!.
Example check: MISSISSIPPI has 11 letters with I = 4, S = 4, P = 2, so ways = 11!/(4! 4! 2!).
Option B (n^k) and option C (n^r) are for arrangements with repetition allowed, not this case.
Option A has extra factors p1, n1! etc. which do not belong in the formula.
Only option D, n!/(p1! p2! ... pk!), is correct.

questions.q: How many signals can be made by arranging AT LEAST 2 flags in a sequence on a vertical staff, from 5 different flags available?
questions.info: Signalling-flag problems like this are a classic application of nPr summed across multiple possible lengths - the same pattern appears in 'number plate' or 'password' counting problems.
questions.trick: Don't try to find one clever combined formula - just compute nPr for each flag-count separately (there are only 4 cases here) and add them up; it's quick enough and less error-prone than searching for a shortcut.
questions.concept: 'At least 2 flags' (out of 5 available) means we must add up the permutations for using 2, 3, 4, AND 5 flags in sequence.
calculation: Flags are different and the order on the staff matters, so use permutations: nPr = n!/(n - r)!.
At least 2 flags means 2, 3, 4 or 5 flags. Add all four cases.
3 flags: 5P3 = 5 x 4 x 3 = 60.

questions.q: A batch has 4 red and 7 green uniform boys. Find ways to pick a squad of 5 with (i) at least 1 red AND 1 green, (ii) at least 3 red.
questions.given: 4 red, 7 green uniform boys; squad size 5.
questions.concept: Total ways to choose r from n is nCr. 'At least 1 of each' = total minus the all-one-colour cases. 'At least 3 red' means summing the 3-red and 4-red cases.
calculation: Formula: nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!). Total boys = 4 + 7 = 11, squad = 5.
(i) At least 1 red and 1 green = Total minus all-red minus all-green.
All red: need 5 red but only 4 exist, so 4C5 = 0.
(ii) At least 3 red = (3 red, 2 green) + (4 red, 1 green). 4C3 x 7C2 = 4 x 21 = 84. 4C4 x 7C1 = 1 x 7 = 7.
(ii) = 84 + 7 = 91. So (i) 441 and (ii) 91, option C.
questions.info: This 'total minus the impossible/extreme cases' trick is the standard way to handle 'at least 1 of each group' combinatorics questions.
questions.trick: Compute the single total nCr first (here 462) - it anchors every other part of a multi-part combinatorics question.

questions.q: If the sum 1! - 2! + 3! - 4! + ...... - 10! is divided by 24, then the remainder will be:
questions.given: Alternating sum of factorials from 1! to 10!, divided by 24.
questions.concept: n! is a multiple of 4! = 24 for every n at least 4, so only the first three terms matter.
calculation: Idea: 4! = 24, so every term n! with n at least 4 is a multiple of 24 and leaves remainder 0.
Terms from 4! to 10! therefore contribute nothing to the remainder.
Only the first three terms remain: 1! - 2! + 3!.
5 is less than 24, so the remainder is 5, which is option C.
questions.info: Same idea gives the last digits of factorial sums: n! ends in 0 for n at least 5, so only 1! to 4! decide the unit digit.
questions.trick: Find the first n where n! is a multiple of the divisor; ignore all terms from there on.
questions.formula: n! divisible by 24 for n at least 4

questions.q: The coefficient of x^12 in the expansion of (3x^2 + 1/x)^30 is:
questions.given: Expansion of (3x^2 + 1/x)^30; find the coefficient of x^12.
questions.concept: General term T(r+1) = nCr * (first)^(n-r) * (second)^r; match the power of x.
calculation: Formula: T(r+1) = nCr * a^(n-r) * b^r with a = 3x^2, b = 1/x, n = 30.
Power of x = 60 - 2r - r = 60 - 3r.
Set 60 - 3r = 12, so 3r = 48 and r = 16.
This is option D.
questions.info: The stem as printed in the image was partly unclear; n = 30 is consistent with the options and the marked answer.
questions.trick: Write the power of x as a linear function of r, solve for r, then read the coefficient. Check r is a whole number between 0 and n.

questions.q: If the determinant of [[1,1,0],[x^2+2x+2,1,0],[2,1,1]] = 0, the value of x is:
questions.given: A 3x3 determinant equation involving x, set equal to 0.
questions.concept: Expand a determinant along the row/column with the most zeros to minimise work - here the third column has only one nonzero entry.
calculation: Matrix rows: (1, 1, 0), (x^2+2x+2, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1). Expand along the 3rd column, which has two zeros.
Only the entry in row 3, column 3 is non-zero (it is 1). Its sign is (-1)^(3+3) = +1.
So det = 1 x (minor after deleting row 3 and column 3) = det of [[1, 1], [x^2+2x+2, 1]].
x = -1, option D. Check: x = -1 gives x^2+2x+2 = 1, rows 1 and 2 become equal, so det = 0.
questions.info: Whenever a matrix row/column has mostly zeros, ALWAYS expand along that row/column - it collapses a 3x3 determinant into a single 2x2 calculation instead of three.
questions.trick: Scan for the row/column with the most zeros before picking an expansion row - saves real computation time, especially under exam pressure.

questions.q: P is a square matrix of order 3 and |P| = -4. Then |adj(P)| equals:
questions.concept: Standard identity: for an n x n matrix, |adj(P)| = |P|^(n-1).
calculation: Formula: for an n x n matrix P, |adj(P)| = |P|^(n-1).
Here the order is 3, so n = 3 and n-1 = 2.
Substitute |P| = -4: |adj(P)| = (-4)^2.
(-4)^2 = (-4) x (-4) = 16 (minus times minus is plus).
So |adj(P)| = 16. Do not stop at -4 or -16: an even power always gives a positive value.
questions.info: This identity comes from P*adj(P)=|P|*I; taking determinants of both sides gives |P|*|adj(P)|=|P|^n, which rearranges to |adj(P)|=|P|^(n-1).
questions.trick: Memorise |adj(P)|=|P|^(n-1) as a direct formula - never recompute the full adjugate matrix just to find its determinant.

questions.q: Matrix A has order (p x q) and matrix B has order (r x s). The product AB exists when:
questions.given: A is (p x q), B is (r x s).
questions.concept: Matrix multiplication rule: AB is defined only when A's column count matches B's row count.
calculation: Rule: AB exists only when columns of A = rows of B.
A has order p x q, so A has q columns.
B has order r x s, so B has r rows.
Condition: q = r.
Check options: r = s is about B being square, p = r compares rows of A with rows of B, q = s compares columns with columns. All three are wrong.
Only q = r matches the rule.
questions.info: If AB is defined, the resulting product matrix has the order (p x s) - the 'outer' dimensions of A and B.
questions.trick: Write the two orders side by side as p x q, r x s - the 'inner' numbers (q,r) must match for the product to exist; the 'outer' numbers (p,s) give the answer's shape.

questions.q: Which of the following matrices is a symmetric matrix?
questions.given: Four candidate 3x3 matrices.
questions.concept: A matrix is symmetric when it equals its own transpose: entry(i,j) = entry(j,i) for every pair.
calculation: Rule: A is symmetric when entry(i,j) = entry(j,i), so only compare mirror pairs [1,2] with [2,1], [1,3] with [3,1], [2,3] with [3,2].
Option A: [1,2] = -3 but [2,1] = 3. Not equal, so not symmetric.
Option C: [1,2] = 3 but [2,1] = -2. Not equal, so not symmetric.
Option D: [1,2] = [2,1] = 3 and [1,3] = [3,1] = 4 match, but [2,3] = -4 and [3,2] = 4. Not equal, so not symmetric.
So the symmetric matrix is [[2,3,4],[3,-3,4],[4,4,4]].
questions.info: The diagonal entries of a symmetric matrix can be ANYTHING - only the off-diagonal mirror pairs need to match each other.
questions.trick: Just check the 3 mirror pairs across the diagonal - don't bother computing the full transpose matrix.

questions.q: Solve the system: 3x+y+5z=30, 2x+2y-3z=40, x+y+2z=20.
questions.given: Three linear equations in x, y, z, with 4 MCQ candidate solutions.
questions.concept: With only 4 options given, substitution-testing each candidate is faster than solving the system algebraically.
calculation: With 4 options, putting each option into the equations is fastest. Test every option in equation 1: 3x + y + 5z = 30.
Option A (0,10,5): 0 + 10 + 25 = 35, not 30. Rejected.
Option C (5,0,15): 15 + 0 + 75 = 90, not 30. Rejected.
Option D (10,5,5): 30 + 5 + 25 = 60, not 30. Rejected.
Option B (5,15,0): 15 + 15 + 0 = 30. Matches, so check the other equations too.
Equation 2: 2x + 2y - 3z = 10 + 30 - 0 = 40. Matches.
Equation 3: x + y + 2z = 5 + 15 + 0 = 20. Matches.
All three equations hold, so x = 5, y = 15, z = 0.
questions.info: This exact problem can also be solved properly via Cramer's rule or the matrix inverse method (A^-1 B) - useful when no answer options are given to test against.
questions.trick: When a 3-equation system comes with 4 MCQ options, substitution-testing is almost always faster than solving the system from scratch - just plug in and check all 3 equations.

questions.q: If |A|=4 and |B|=5 for square matrices A,B, what is |AB|?
questions.given: |A|=4, |B|=5, both square matrices of the same order.
questions.concept: Key determinant property: |AB| = |A| * |B| for any two square matrices of the same order.
calculation: Formula: |AB| = |A| x |B| (A and B are square matrices of the same order).
Substitute |A| = 4 and |B| = 5.
Do not add (9) or square (16, 25): determinants multiply.
questions.info: This multiplicative property does NOT extend to addition - |A+B| is generally NOT equal to |A|+|B|, a common trap to watch for.
questions.trick: Spot 'given |A| and |B|, find |AB|' instantly as a one-line multiplication - no matrix construction needed.

questions.q: Express the matrix A=[[4,2,-3],[1,3,-6],[-5,0,-7]] as sum of symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices.
questions.concept: Standard decomposition: any square matrix A = (symmetric part) + (skew-symmetric part), where symmetric part = (A+A^T)/2 and skew-symmetric part = (A-A^T)/2.
calculation: Formula: A = (A + A^T)/2 + (A - A^T)/2. The first part is symmetric, the second is skew-symmetric.
Write A^T by swapping rows and columns: A^T = [[4,1,-5],[2,3,0],[-3,-6,-7]].
A - A^T = [[0,1,2],[-1,0,-6],[-2,6,0]] (subtract matching entries).
Half of it: Q = (A - A^T)/2 = [[0,0.5,1],[-0.5,0,-3],[-1,3,0]]. Diagonal is 0 and Q^T = -Q, so skew-symmetric.
Check one entry: P[1,2] + Q[1,2] = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2 = A[1,2]. Good.
questions.info: A skew-symmetric matrix ALWAYS has zeros on its main diagonal, since entry(i,i) must equal its own negative - a quick way to sanity-check your (A-A^T)/2 computation.
questions.trick: Compute A^T first, then just add/subtract and halve - no need to solve for unknowns or set up equations, it's a direct formula.

questions.q: If A and B are symmetric matrices of the same order, then (AB' - BA') is:
questions.given: A and B symmetric, same order; classify AB' - BA'.
questions.concept: Symmetric means A' = A. A matrix X is skew symmetric if X' = -X.
calculation: Symmetric means A' = A and B' = B, so AB' - BA' = AB - BA.
Let X = AB - BA.
Use A' = A and B' = B: X' = BA - AB.
BA - AB = -(AB - BA) = -X.
X' = -X, so X is skew symmetric. Matches option A.
questions.info: For symmetric A and B, the product AB is symmetric only when AB = BA (they commute).
questions.trick: Commutator AB - BA of symmetric matrices is always skew symmetric.

questions.given: Two equal 2x2 matrices; compare entries.
questions.concept: Equal matrices have equal corresponding entries.
calculation: Equal matrices: compare each entry. 2x + y = 7 ... (1) and 4x = 7y - 13 ... (2).
From (4): 4x - x = 6, so 3x = 6 and x = 2.
x + y = 2 + 3 = 5. Matches option C.
questions.info: A system from matrix equality may be overdetermined; use a consistent pair and check the rest.
questions.trick: Pick the equation with a single unknown first (here 4x = x + 6) to start.

questions.q: Let Delta = |[Ax, x^2, 1],[By, y^2, 1],[Cz, z^2, 1]| and Delta_1 = |[A, B, C],[x, y, z],[zy, zx, xy]|, then
questions.given: Delta has rows (Ax,x^2,1),(By,y^2,1),(Cz,z^2,1); Delta_1 has rows (A,B,C),(x,y,z),(zy,zx,xy).
questions.concept: Transpose keeps a determinant; multiplying a row by k multiplies it by k; a common column factor can be taken out.
calculation: Transpose Delta_1 (value unchanged): rows become (A,x,zy),(B,y,zx),(C,z,xy).
Multiply row 1 by x, row 2 by y and row 3 by z. Determinant becomes xyz x Delta_1.
Rows become (Ax,x^2,xyz),(By,y^2,xyz),(Cz,z^2,xyz).
Take xyz common from column 3: xyz x |[Ax,x^2,1],[By,y^2,1],[Cz,z^2,1]| = xyz x Delta.
So xyz x Delta_1 = xyz x Delta.
Cancel xyz (nonzero in general): Delta_1 = Delta, so Delta_1 - Delta = 0. Matches option C.
questions.info: Row or column scaling is a standard way to match two different-looking determinants.
questions.trick: Try making a column of Delta_1 match Delta by multiplying rows by x, y, z.

questions.concept: Compute A^2 and A^3 to see the pattern, then confirm by induction.
calculation: Formula: A^n = A * A^(n-1); find the pattern from small powers.
The top-right entry goes 2, 4, 6, so it is 2n for A^n.
This matches option C.
questions.info: For an upper-triangular matrix [[1,a],[0,1]], A^n = [[1,n*a],[0,1]] for every positive integer n.
questions.trick: Test n = 1: only [[1,2n],[0,1]] gives 2 in the corner. Options A and B fail; option D fails with 1 versus 2.

questions.q: The pair of linear equations in two variables x and y, 29x + 37y + 7 = 0 and 87x + 74y + 5 = 0 will have:
questions.concept: Compare a1/a2 with b1/b2: if different, the lines intersect at exactly one point.
calculation: Formula: for a1*x + b1*y + c1 = 0 and a2*x + b2*y + c2 = 0, unique solution when a1/a2 is not equal to b1/b2.
1/3 is not equal to 1/2, so the lines are neither parallel nor coincident.
They cut at exactly one point, so the system has a unique solution, which is option C.
questions.info: Same ratio gives a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2 for infinite solutions, and a1/a2 = b1/b2 but not c1/c2 for no solution. 'Trivial solution' applies only to homogeneous systems.
questions.trick: Only compare the x and y coefficient ratios first. If they differ, stop: unique solution.
questions.formula: a1/a2 not equal to b1/b2 means unique solution

questions.q: The value of k, for which the following system of linear equations has a non-trivial solution, x + 2y - 3z = 0, 2x + y + z = 0, x - y + kz = 0 will be:
questions.given: Homogeneous system: x + 2y - 3z = 0, 2x + y + z = 0, x - y + kz = 0.
questions.concept: A homogeneous system has a non-trivial solution only if the determinant of coefficients is zero.
calculation: A non-trivial solution exists only when the coefficient determinant is 0.
First term: 1*(k + 1) = k + 1.
Second term: -2*(2k - 1) = -4k + 2.
Third term: -3*(-2 - 1) = 9.
12 - 3k = 0 gives k = 4, which is option A.
questions.info: If the determinant is non-zero the only solution is x = y = z = 0 (trivial). If zero, there are infinitely many solutions.
questions.trick: For homogeneous systems, never solve the equations. Just set the determinant to zero.

questions.concept: Expand the 3x3 determinant along the first row.
calculation: Formula: expand along row 1 with cofactor signs +, -, +.
|A| = 0 + (1 + i) + (1 - i) = 2. Matches option C.
questions.info: Remember i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1 when simplifying complex entries.
questions.trick: Convert every product of i's to plain numbers immediately; the imaginary parts cancel at the end.

questions.concept: Adjoint = transpose of the cofactor matrix.
calculation: Formula: adj(A) = transpose of the matrix of cofactors C_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij.
Transpose it: adj(A) = [[-5,-5,4],[2,1,-1],[4,4,-3]]. Matches option A.
questions.info: Option B is the cofactor matrix itself; forgetting the transpose is the classic trap.
questions.trick: Check quickly: A*adj(A) must equal |A| times I; first entry gives 1*(-5)+1*2+1*4 = 1, so |A| = 1.

questions.q: What are the coordinates of the image of the point (2,3) in the line (acting as a mirror) x + 3y = 5?
questions.given: Point (2,3), mirror line x+3y=5.
questions.concept: Reflection formula for a point (x1,y1) in the line ax+by+c=0: reflected point = (x1,y1) - [2(ax1+by1+c)/(a^2+b^2)] * (a,b).
calculation: Formula: image of (x1,y1) in line ax + by + c = 0 is (x1,y1) - [2(a x1 + b y1 + c)/(a^2 + b^2)] x (a,b).
Write the line as x + 3y - 5 = 0. So a = 1, b = 3, c = -5.
Point is (x1,y1) = (2,3).
questions.info: The midpoint of a point and its mirror image always lies exactly ON the mirror line - a quick way to verify your answer: midpoint of (2,3) and (4/5,-3/5) is (7/5, 6/5), check it satisfies x+3y=5: 7/5+18/5=25/5=5, confirmed.
questions.trick: Memorise the reflection formula as a single template and just plug in a,b,c,x1,y1 - don't re-derive it from perpendicular-line geometry each time.

questions.q: What is the equation of a line through (-3,8) perpendicular to 3x+y=8?
questions.given: Point (-3,8), given line 3x+y=8.
questions.concept: Perpendicular slopes always multiply to -1 (m1*m2=-1); use point-slope form once the perpendicular slope is known.
calculation: Formula: slopes of perpendicular lines satisfy m1 x m2 = -1.
Write 3x + y = 8 as y = -3x + 8. So its slope m1 = -3.
Perpendicular slope m2 = -1/m1 = -1/(-3) = 1/3.
Point-slope form through (-3,8): y - 8 = m2 (x - (-3)) = (1/3)(x + 3).
Multiply both sides by 3: 3(y - 8) = x + 3.
Move everything to one side: x - 3y + 3 + 24 = 0, which is x - 3y + 27 = 0.
Quick check: put (-3,8): -3 - 24 + 27 = 0. True, so the line passes through the point.
questions.info: Perpendicular slopes always multiply to -1 (m1*m2=-1) - this is the single fact this entire question tests.
questions.trick: For 'perpendicular line through a point' questions, just flip-and-negate the given slope, then plug straight into point-slope form - 2 lines of algebra, no need for distance or angle formulas.

questions.q: If the lines x + 2y + 1 = 0, 8x + 12y + k = 0, 3x - 2y + 5 = 0 are concurrent, then the value of k is:
questions.given: Three lines meeting at one point.
questions.concept: Find the intersection of two lines, then substitute it in the third line.
calculation: Take the lines without k: x + 2y + 1 = 0 and 3x - 2y + 5 = 0.
Add them: 4x + 6 = 0, so x = -3/2.
Intersection point is (-3/2, 1/4).
-12 + 3 + k = 0, so k = 9, which is option C.
questions.info: Equivalent test: the determinant of the coefficients [[1,2,1],[8,12,k],[3,-2,5]] equals zero.
questions.trick: Choose the two lines where adding or subtracting removes a variable immediately.
questions.formula: Point common to all three lines satisfies each equation

questions.q: For what value of alpha + beta, the three points (alpha, beta), (5,0), (0,5) will be collinear?
questions.given: Points (alpha, beta), (5, 0), (0, 5) are collinear; find alpha + beta.
questions.concept: Collinear points lie on one line; the line through (5,0) and (0,5) is x/5 + y/5 = 1.
calculation: Formula: intercept form of a line, x/a + y/b = 1.
The line through (5, 0) and (0, 5) has x-intercept 5 and y-intercept 5.
So its equation is x/5 + y/5 = 1, i.e. x + y = 5.
Collinear means (alpha, beta) lies on this line.
Put x = alpha, y = beta: alpha + beta = 5.
This is option A.
questions.info: Area-of-triangle test gives the same result: (1/2)|alpha(0-5) + 5(5-beta) + 0| = 0 gives alpha + beta = 5.
questions.trick: Two intercept points (a,0) and (0,a) always give the line x + y = a, so any third point on it has coordinate sum a.

questions.q: What is the equation of the straight line passing through (-2,-1) and having inclination 150 degrees?
questions.given: Point (-2,-1), inclination 150 degrees.
questions.concept: Slope = tan(inclination); then point-slope form.
calculation: Formula: slope m = tan(theta), and y - y1 = m(x - x1).
m = tan150 = -tan30 = -1/sqrt(3).
Multiply by sqrt(3): sqrt(3)y + sqrt(3) = -x - 2.
Bring all terms to the left: x + sqrt(3)y + 2 + sqrt(3) = 0. Matches option C.
questions.info: Inclination is the angle the line makes with the positive x-axis, measured anticlockwise, so an obtuse angle means negative slope.
questions.trick: An obtuse inclination gives negative slope, so x and y coefficients must have the same sign: only option C fits.

questions.q: What is the distance from the origin to the line 3x + 4y + 5 = 0?
questions.given: Line 3x + 4y + 5 = 0; point (0,0).
questions.concept: Perpendicular distance from a point to a line.
calculation: Formula: d = |a*x1 + b*y1 + c|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
Denominator = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5.
d = 5/5 = 1. Matches option D.
questions.info: For the origin, distance is just |c|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2), no substitution needed.
questions.trick: The 3-4-5 triple appears here; denominator is 5 straight away.

questions.q: What is the equation of an ellipse with focus at (3,0) and major axis length 10?
questions.given: Focus at (3,0), major axis length = 10.
questions.concept: Ellipse relation: c^2 = a^2 - b^2, where 2a=major axis length and c=distance from centre to focus.
calculation: Formula: ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 (major axis along x) with c^2 = a^2 - b^2.
Major axis length = 2a = 10, so a = 5 and a^2 = 25.
Focus (3,0) lies on the x-axis, so the major axis is along x and c = 3, c^2 = 9.
Substitute: 9 = 25 - b^2.
Option check: option A has a minus sign (hyperbola), so wrong. Option D has the bigger denominator under y^2 (major axis along y), so wrong. x^2/9 + y^2/10 = 1 has a^2 = 10, not 25, so wrong.
Equation: x^2/25 + y^2/16 = 1.
questions.info: For an ellipse, a > b always, and the LARGER denominator tells you which axis (x or y) is the major axis - here 25>16 confirms the major axis is indeed along x, consistent with the given focus on the x-axis.
questions.trick: Memorise c^2=a^2-b^2 as the core ellipse relation (different from hyperbola's c^2=a^2+b^2) - most ellipse MCQs reduce to finding a^2 and b^2 then plugging into the standard form.

questions.q: Equation of hyperbola whose asymptotes are 3x +- 5y = 0 and vertices are (+-5, 0) is
questions.given: Asymptotes 3x +- 5y = 0; vertices (+-5, 0).
questions.concept: Hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 has vertices (+-a, 0) and asymptotes y = +-(b/a)x.
calculation: Formula: x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1, vertices (+-a, 0), asymptotes y = +-(b/a)x.
Vertices (+-5, 0) give a = 5.
Asymptotes 3x +- 5y = 0 give y = +-(3/5)x, so b/a = 3/5.
Equation: x^2/25 - y^2/9 = 1.
Multiply by 225: 9x^2 - 25y^2 = 225.
This matches option A.
questions.info: Asymptotes of x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 come from setting the right side to 0, i.e. x/a +- y/b = 0.
questions.trick: Use the asymptote form x/5 +- y/3 = 0, which is 3x +- 5y = 0 scaled; so a = 5 and b = 3 directly.

questions.q: The line y = 2x + b is a tangent to the parabola y^2 = 8x, if:
questions.given: Line y = 2x + b (slope m = 2), parabola y^2 = 8x.
questions.concept: Line y = mx + c touches y^2 = 4ax if c = a/m.
calculation: Formula: the line y = mx + c is tangent to y^2 = 4ax when c = a/m.
Compare y^2 = 8x with y^2 = 4ax: 4a = 8, so a = 2.
From the line y = 2x + b: m = 2 and c = b.
Apply the condition: b = a/m = 2/2.
b = 1, which is option D.
Check: substitute y = 2x + 1 into y^2 = 8x: 4x^2 + 4x + 1 = 8x gives 4x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0, discriminant 16 - 16 = 0, so it touches.
questions.info: The point of contact of y = mx + a/m on y^2 = 4ax is (a/m^2, 2a/m). Here it is (1/2, 2).
questions.trick: Tangent to y^2 = 4ax is always y = mx + a/m: find a from the coefficient of x, then c = a/m directly.

questions.q: Let f(x,y)=0 represents a circle. If f(0,a) has roots a=2,3 and f(a,0) has roots a=12, 1/2, then the centre of the circle is:
questions.given: Circle x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0; f(0,a) has roots 2 and 3; f(a,0) has roots 12 and 1/2.
questions.concept: Putting x = 0 gives the y-intercept quadratic, putting y = 0 gives the x-intercept quadratic; use sum of roots.
calculation: Formula: circle x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f).
Put x = 0: y^2 + 2fy + c = 0 with roots 2 and 3.
Sum of roots = 2 + 3 = 5 = -2f, so f = -5/2.
Put y = 0: x^2 + 2gx + c = 0 with roots 12 and 1/2.
Check: product of roots is c = 6 in both cases (2 x 3 and 12 x 1/2), consistent. This is option D.
questions.info: The product of the roots is c in both quadratics, giving a free consistency check (power of the origin).
questions.trick: Centre x-coordinate is half the sum of the x-intercepts, and centre y is half the sum of the y-intercepts.

questions.q: What is the focus of the parabola y^2 - x - 2y + 2 = 0?
questions.given: Parabola y^2 - x - 2y + 2 = 0.
questions.concept: Complete the square to get (y-k)^2 = 4a(x-h); focus (h+a, k).
calculation: Formula: (y-k)^2 = 4a(x-h) has vertex (h,k) and focus (h+a, k).
Rearrange: y^2 - 2y = x - 2.
Complete the square: y^2 - 2y + 1 = x - 2 + 1, so (y-1)^2 = x - 1.
Compare: h = 1, k = 1, 4a = 1, so a = 1/4.
Vertex = (1,1). Opens to the right since a is positive.
Focus = (h + a, k) = (1 + 1/4, 1) = (5/4, 1). Matches option A.
questions.info: For a parabola opening right, the directrix is x = h - a, here x = 3/4.
questions.trick: Complete the square first; then focus is vertex shifted by a along the axis of symmetry.

questions.q: If f is differentiable at x=c and one-one near c, g is the inverse of f, then g'{f(c)} is:
questions.given: g is the inverse of f, f is differentiable and one-one near c.
questions.concept: Inverse Function Theorem: if g is the inverse of f, then g'(f(c)) = 1/f'(c), valid wherever f'(c) is not zero.
calculation: Formula: if g is the inverse of f, then g(f(x)) = x for all x near c.
Differentiate both sides using the chain rule: g'(f(x)) x f'(x) = 1.
Put x = c: g'(f(c)) x f'(c) = 1.
Divide both sides by f'(c) (allowed only when f'(c) is not 0): g'(f(c)) = 1/f'(c).
Option check: option B is a product-rule expression, option C is just f'(c), option D is f(c)/f'(c). None of these satisfy g'(f(c)) x f'(c) = 1.
So g'(f(c)) = 1/f'(c), where f'(c) is not 0.
questions.info: Geometrically, the graph of an inverse function is the reflection of the original across y=x - so slopes become reciprocals, matching the formula.
questions.trick: Recognise 'inverse function derivative' questions instantly - the answer is always 1/f'(c), never anything more complicated.

questions.q: Find dy/dx given the implicit equation x^2+y^2=a^2.
questions.given: x^2+y^2=a^2 (equation of a circle), find dy/dx.
questions.concept: Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, applying the chain rule to y-terms (multiply by dy/dx).
calculation: Rule: differentiate both sides with respect to x. For y terms use the chain rule: d/dx(y^2) = 2y x dy/dx.
Equation: x^2 + y^2 = a^2.
d/dx(y^2) = 2y (dy/dx).
d/dx(a^2) = 0, because a is a constant.
So 2x + 2y (dy/dx) = 0.
Move 2x across: 2y (dy/dx) = -2x.
Divide by 2y: dy/dx = -x/y.
Check: slope of a circle at (x,y) is perpendicular to the radius slope y/x, so it is -x/y. Matches.
questions.info: This is the equation of a circle of radius a - the result dy/dx=-x/y matches the geometric fact that the tangent to a circle is always perpendicular to its radius.
questions.trick: For implicit differentiation, always remember: every time you differentiate a y-term, multiply by dy/dx (chain rule) - this is the single most common place students lose marks.

questions.q: At which point is f(x) = [x] (greatest integer function) continuous?
questions.given: f(x)=[x], the greatest integer (floor) function; 4 candidate points.
questions.concept: [x] is discontinuous at every integer (it jumps by 1 there) and continuous everywhere else.
calculation: Rule: [x] is the greatest integer function. It jumps at every integer, so it is discontinuous at every integer and continuous at all other points.
x = 3.6: not an integer. Left and right limits are both [3.6] = 3. Continuous.
x = -4: integer. Left limit is -5, right limit is -4. Jump, so discontinuous.
x = 3: integer. Left limit is 2, right limit is 3. Jump, so discontinuous.
x = 0: integer. Left limit is -1, right limit is 0. Jump, so discontinuous.
So f(x) = [x] is continuous at x = 3.6.
questions.info: The greatest integer function's graph looks like a staircase - continuous along each flat step, but discontinuous at every step edge (each integer).
questions.trick: For [x]-type continuity questions, just check if the given point is an integer or not - integers are always discontinuous, everything else is always continuous.

questions.q: f(x) = {(sin x)/x + sec(x), x not 0; a, x=0}. For continuity at x=0, what is a?
questions.given: f(x) = sin(x)/x + sec(x) for x≠0, f(0)=a. Need a for continuity.
questions.concept: For continuity at x=0, the defined value 'a' must equal the limit of f(x) as x approaches 0.
calculation: Condition: f is continuous at 0 when a = f(0) = limit of f(x) as x goes to 0.
limit of f(x) = limit of sin(x)/x + limit of sec(x) (limit of a sum is the sum of limits).
Standard limit: limit of sin(x)/x as x goes to 0 = 1.
sec(x) = 1/cos(x), and cos(0) = 1, so limit of sec(x) = 1/1 = 1.
Limit = 1 + 1 = 2.
So a = 2.
questions.info: lim(sinx/x)=1 as x->0 is one of the most frequently reused limits in calculus - memorise it cold, it appears in dozens of problem variations.
questions.trick: Whenever a piecewise function asks for a continuity-constant like 'a', just compute the limit of the other piece as x approaches that point - that's always the answer.

questions.q: What is the limit as x approaches 12 of (x^3 - 1728)/(x-12)?
questions.concept: Standard limit form: lim(x->a) (x^n-a^n)/(x-a) = n*a^(n-1).
calculation: Formula: limit as x goes to a of (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n x a^(n-1).
The limit becomes (x^3 - 12^3)/(x - 12), so n = 3 and a = 12.
Substitute: n x a^(n-1) = 3 x 12^2.
Check: direct substitution gives 0/0, so we need the formula (or factorising). Answer 432.
questions.info: This standard limit formula n*a^(n-1) is exactly the definition of the derivative of x^n at x=a - this limit question is secretly asking you to differentiate x^3.
questions.trick: Spot the (x^n-a^n)/(x-a) pattern immediately and apply n*a^(n-1) directly - never try to factor or use L'Hopital's rule for this, it's slower.

questions.q: If f(x) = 4*cos(x^3)/sin(x), what is f'(x)?
questions.given: f(x) = 4cos(x^3)/sin(x).
questions.concept: Quotient rule: f'(x) = [u'v - uv']/v^2, where u=4cos(x^3), v=sin(x).
calculation: Formula (quotient rule): f' = (u'v - u v')/v^2 with u = 4cos(x^3) and v = sin(x).
Find u' using the chain rule: derivative of cos(x^3) is -sin(x^3) x 3x^2. So u' = 4 x (-sin(x^3)) x 3x^2 = -12x^2 sin(x^3).
v' = cos(x).
Substitute: f' = [-12x^2 sin(x^3) sin(x) - 4cos(x^3) cos(x)] / sin^2(x).
Split into two fractions: first = -12x^2 sin(x^3) sin(x)/sin^2(x) = -12x^2 sin(x^3)/sin(x) = -12x^2 sin(x^3) cosec(x).
Second = -4cos(x^3) cos(x)/sin^2(x) = -4cos(x^3) x [1/sin(x)] x [cos(x)/sin(x)] = -4cos(x^3) cosec(x) cot(x).
Option check: option A has sin(x^2) and sec(x), so wrong. The other two lack the second term, so wrong.
f'(x) = -12x^2 sin(x^3) cosec(x) - 4cos(x^3) cosec(x) cot(x).
questions.info: Writing final trig-derivative answers using cosec/cot (instead of leaving them as fractions over sin/cos) is the conventional textbook style - exam answer keys usually expect this form.
questions.trick: After applying quotient rule, immediately split into two separate fractions over v^2 rather than keeping one combined fraction - it's much easier to simplify into cosec/cot form term by term.

questions.q: If f(x) = 3x^2*sin(x) + tan(x), what is f'(x)?
questions.given: f(x) = 3x^2*sin(x) + tan(x).
questions.concept: Differentiate term by term (sum rule); the first term needs the product rule, the second is a standard derivative.
calculation: Rule: differentiate term by term. f(x) = 3x^2 sin(x) + tan(x).
First term needs the product rule: (uv)' = u'v + uv' with u = 3x^2 and v = sin(x).
u' = 6x and v' = cos(x).
d/dx(3x^2 sin(x)) = 6x sin(x) + 3x^2 cos(x).
Standard derivative: d/dx(tan(x)) = sec^2(x).
Option check: option A has cot^2(x), which is wrong. Options B and D miss the product-rule terms.
Add both parts: f'(x) = 6x sin(x) + 3x^2 cos(x) + sec^2(x).
questions.info: d/dx(tan x)=sec^2(x) and d/dx(cot x)=-cosec^2(x) are easy to mix up under pressure - note the sign difference and which reciprocal function pairs with which.
questions.trick: Split sums into separate derivative terms FIRST, then handle the trickier product-rule term in isolation - don't try to differentiate the whole expression in one pass.

questions.q: What is the limit as x approaches 0 of (sin(2x) - tan(2x))/x^3?
questions.given: lim(x->0) of (sin(2x)-tan(2x))/x^3.
questions.concept: Use small-angle Taylor series: sin(u) ≈ u - u^3/6, tan(u) ≈ u + u^3/3, for small u.
calculation: Direct substitution gives 0/0, so use the series for small u: sin(u) = u - u^3/6 and tan(u) = u + u^3/3 (higher powers are ignored).
Put u = 2x. Then (2x)^3 = 8x^3.
Subtract: sin(2x) - tan(2x) = (2x - 2x) + (-4x^3/3 - 8x^3/3).
Divide by x^3: (-4x^3)/x^3 = -4.
Limit = -4.
questions.info: This Taylor-series approach is much faster than repeated L'Hopital's rule for 0/0-type limits involving sin/tan/cos - worth memorising the first 2 terms of sin(u), cos(u), tan(u) series.
questions.trick: For any 0/0 limit with sin/tan/cos divided by a power of x, substitute the small-angle series directly instead of differentiating 3 times with L'Hopital's rule - far fewer steps.
questions.formula: sin(u) approx u-u^3/6, tan(u) approx u+u^3/3

questions.q: The function f(x) = (4 - x^2)/(4x - x^3) is
questions.concept: A rational function is discontinuous where its denominator is zero (f undefined there).
calculation: Find where the denominator is zero: 4x - x^3 = 0.
Roots: x = 0, x = 2, x = -2.
At each of these points f is not defined, so f is discontinuous there.
Note (4 - x^2) cancels for other x, giving f = 1/x, but the original function is still undefined at x = 2 and x = -2.
Three points of discontinuity. Matches option C.
questions.info: Cancelling a common factor does not repair the domain; x = 2 and x = -2 are removable discontinuities.
questions.trick: Count the real roots of the denominator before simplifying.

questions.q: If y = (1+x)(1+x^2)......(1+x^100) then dy/dx at x = 0 is
questions.concept: Product rule via logarithmic differentiation: y'/y = sum of (derivative of each factor)/(factor).
calculation: Formula: take ln, so ln y = sum of ln(1 + x^k) for k = 1 to 100.
Differentiate: y'/y = sum of k*x^(k-1)/(1 + x^k).
For k = 1 the term is 1/(1+0) = 1.
For k = 2 to 100 the term has x^(k-1) with k-1 at least 1, so it is 0 at x = 0.
This matches option C.
questions.info: The same idea shows the coefficient of x in the expansion of the product is 1, because only (1+x) contributes a linear term.
questions.trick: At x = 0 only the factor (1+x) can give a first-power term, so the derivative is just 1 times the product of the other factors, which is 1.
questions.formula: y'/y = sum of k*x^(k-1)/(1+x^k), k = 1 to 100

questions.q: Evaluate limit as x tends to infinity of ((x+1)/(x+2))^(2x+1)
questions.given: Limit as x tends to infinity of ((x+1)/(x+2))^(2x+1).
questions.concept: 1-infinity form: lim (1 + f)^g = e^(lim f*g) when f tends to 0 and g tends to infinity.
