questions.trick: Find the intersection first from the union formula; everything else is one division.

questions.q: If a die is thrown, then the probability of getting a number greater than or equal to 3 is:
questions.given: One fair die; event: number at least 3.
questions.concept: Probability = favourable/total outcomes.
calculation: Formula: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.
Sample space S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, so n(S) = 6.
Favourable outcomes (at least 3) = {3,4,5,6}, so n(E) = 4.
= 2/3. Matches option A.
questions.info: Complement check: P(less than 3) = 2/6 = 1/3, and 1 - 1/3 = 2/3.
questions.trick: Count the excluded outcomes if fewer: only 1 and 2 are out, so 1 - 2/6.

questions.q: Solve the inequality 8x + 2 >= 2x + 14, x real.
questions.concept: Solve a linear inequality like an equation, but flip the sign only when multiplying/dividing by a negative.
calculation: Given: 8x + 2 greater than or equal to 2x + 14.
Subtract 2x from both sides: 6x + 2 is at least 14.
Subtract 2 from both sides: 6x is at least 12.
Divide both sides by 6 (positive number, so the sign does not flip): x is at least 2.
So x greater than or equal to 2, which is x in [2, infinity).
Square bracket at 2 because 2 is included (sign is greater than or equal). Matches option C.
questions.info: The ONLY rule to watch in inequalities: flip the inequality sign if you multiply or divide both sides by a NEGATIVE number - here we divided by positive 6, so no flip needed.
questions.trick: Solve inequalities exactly like equations (isolate x), and only pause to think about sign-flipping at the final division/multiplication step.

questions.q: Solve the inequality 6x + 7 <= x - 28, x a natural number.
questions.given: 6x+7 <= x-28, x a natural number.
questions.concept: Solve the inequality first, then check if any natural number actually satisfies the resulting range.
calculation: Given: 6x + 7 less than or equal to x - 28, and x is a natural number.
Subtract x from both sides: 5x + 7 is at most -28.
Subtract 7 from both sides: 5x is at most -35.
Divide both sides by 5 (positive, no flip): x is at most -7.
Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3, ... and all are positive.
No positive number is less than or equal to -7.
So there is no solution. (Options x at least 5, x at least 3 fail; x at most -5 is not natural.)
questions.info: Always re-check the DOMAIN restriction (real vs natural vs integer) stated in the question after solving - the algebra can be correct but still yield 'no solution' if the domain excludes every value in the solved range.
questions.trick: Solve the inequality algebraically first without worrying about the domain, then apply the domain restriction as a final filter - trying to track both at once invites errors.

questions.q: A company's cost is C = 300 + 1.5x, revenue is R = 2x. How many toys must be sold for profit?
questions.given: Cost C = 300+1.5x, Revenue R = 2x; find x for profit.
questions.concept: Profit occurs when Revenue > Cost.
calculation: Profit happens when Revenue is greater than Cost.
Write: R greater than C.
2x greater than 300 + 1.5x.
Subtract 1.5x from both sides: 0.5x greater than 300.
Divide both sides by 0.5 (same as multiplying by 2): x greater than 600.
Check: at x = 600, cost = 300 + 900 = 1200 and revenue = 1200, no profit. So more than 600 toys are needed.
questions.info: This is the classic break-even-point setup - the value where R=C (here x=600) is the break-even point; profit needs STRICTLY more units sold than that.
questions.trick: Set Revenue > Cost directly as the inequality - don't compute profit = R-C separately first, it's an unnecessary extra step.

questions.q: Which pair are consecutive odd positive integers both smaller than 14, with sum more than 20?
questions.given: Two consecutive odd positive integers, both < 14, sum > 20.
questions.concept: Represent consecutive odd integers as x and x+2, then set up both inequalities.
calculation: Let the two consecutive odd positive integers be x and x + 2.
Condition 1: both are smaller than 14. The bigger one is x + 2, so x + 2 less than 14, giving x less than 12.
Condition 2: sum is more than 20. x + (x + 2) greater than 20, so 2x + 2 greater than 20.
Subtract 2: 2x greater than 18. Divide by 2: x greater than 9.
So 9 less than x less than 12, and x must be odd.
Odd numbers between 9 and 12: only 11. So x = 11 and x + 2 = 13.
Check: 11 + 13 = 24, which is more than 20, and both are less than 14. (9, 11) fails since 9 + 11 = 20 is not more than 20. Pair is (11, 13).
questions.info: Representing consecutive odd/even integers as x and x+2 (rather than x and x+1) is the standard setup - it automatically keeps both numbers the same parity.
questions.trick: Convert both conditions (sum range AND upper bound) into inequalities on the SAME variable x first, then intersect the ranges - much cleaner than guessing pairs.

questions.concept: Clear all denominators by multiplying through by their LCM, then solve the resulting linear inequality.
calculation: Given: (2-x)/5 - (2-3x)/4 less than or equal to (2x-1)/3.
LCM of 5, 4, 3 is 60. Multiply every term by 60 (positive, so sign stays).
Expand: 24 - 12x - 30 + 45x is at most 40x - 20.
Simplify left side: 33x - 6 is at most 40x - 20.
Subtract 33x from both sides: -6 is at most 7x - 20.
Add 20 to both sides: 14 is at most 7x. Divide by 7: x is at least 2.
So x in [2, infinity).
questions.info: Multiplying by the LCM of all denominators in one single step (rather than clearing them one at a time) keeps the algebra much cleaner and less error-prone.
questions.trick: Find the LCM of ALL denominators up front and multiply through once - trying to clear fractions one at a time usually leads to arithmetic slips.

questions.q: If the ratio of surface area to volume of a cuboid is sqrt(3), then the sum of reciprocals of the three sides (length, breadth and height) of the cuboid will be:
questions.given: Cuboid with sides l, b, h; (surface area)/(volume) = sqrt(3); find 1/l + 1/b + 1/h.
questions.concept: Surface area 2(lb + bh + hl) divided by volume lbh splits into reciprocals of the sides.
calculation: Formula: surface area S = 2(lb + bh + hl) and volume V = lbh.
S/V = 2(lb + bh + hl)/(lbh).
Divide each term by lbh: (lb)/(lbh) = 1/h, (bh)/(lbh) = 1/l, (hl)/(lbh) = 1/b.
Given S/V = sqrt(3): 2(1/l + 1/b + 1/h) = sqrt(3).
sin(pi/3) = sqrt(3)/2, so the answer is option D.
questions.info: For a cube of side a, S/V = 6/a, so S/V = sqrt(3) would mean a = 2*sqrt(3).
questions.trick: Whenever S/V of a cuboid appears, think 'twice the sum of reciprocals of the sides'. Then convert the answer to a trig value like sqrt(3)/2.

questions.q: The linear equation in two variables x and y, 6x + 22y = 14 will have:
questions.given: Single linear equation 6x + 22y = 14 in two unknowns.
questions.concept: One equation in two unknowns has infinitely many solutions; integer ones exist if gcd(a,b) divides c.
calculation: Divide by 2: 3x + 11y = 7.
One equation with two unknowns has infinitely many solutions, so options C and D are wrong.
gcd(3, 11) = 1, and 1 divides 7, so integer solutions exist.
Check one: take y = 2, then 3x = 7 - 22 = -15, so x = -5.
So integer-valued solutions exist, which is option B.
questions.info: Integer solutions of ax + by = c exist exactly when gcd(a,b) divides c, and then they form an infinite family (x0 + (b/g)t, y0 - (a/g)t).
questions.trick: Find one integer pair by trial and you can reject 'no integer solution' at once.

questions.q: The solution of 3(x-2)/5 at most 5(2-x)/3 is:
questions.given: Inequality: 3(x-2)/5 at most 5(2-x)/3.
questions.concept: Clear fractions, collect terms; multiplying by positive keeps the sign.
calculation: Multiply both sides by 15 (positive, so sign stays): 9(x-2) at most 25(2-x).
Expand: 9x - 18 at most 50 - 25x.
Add 25x to both sides: 34x - 18 at most 50.
Add 18: 34x at most 68.
Divide by 34: x at most 2.
Solution set = (-inf, 2], with 2 included. Matches option A.
questions.info: Infinity is never included, so a square bracket next to inf (as in option B) is always wrong.
questions.trick: Notice 5(2-x) = -5(x-2): then 3(x-2)/5 + 5(x-2)/3 at most 0 gives x-2 at most 0 straight away.
questions.formula: a*x at most b, a greater than 0 gives x at most b/a

questions.q: 5^n - 5 is divisible by which number, for all n?
questions.given: Expression 5^n - 5, for all natural n.
questions.concept: Test small values of n to find the pattern, since this isn't a strict induction proof requirement but an MCQ.
calculation: Test the options by putting small values of n in 5^n - 5.
n = 1: 5 - 5 = 0. Zero is divisible by every number, so it tells nothing.
n = 2: 25 - 5 = 20. 20 / 11, 20 / 9, 20 / 7 are not whole numbers. 20 / 4 = 5 is whole.
So 11, 9 and 7 fail. Only 4 is left.
n = 3: 125 - 5 = 120. 120 / 4 = 30, whole number. Good.
Reason: 5^n - 5 = (5^n - 1) - 4, and 5 - 1 = 4 divides 5^n - 1 always. So 4 divides 5^n - 5 for all n.
questions.info: This generalises: a^n - a is always divisible by (a-1) for any base a (here 5-1=4) - a nice shortcut that follows from factoring out a common term.
questions.trick: For 'always divisible by' MCQs, just test n=2 and n=3 (skip n=1, which is often trivially 0) against each option - the one that divides both is almost certainly the answer.

questions.q: For all natural numbers n, n(n+1)(2n+1) is divisible by:
questions.given: Expression n(n+1)(2n+1), for all natural n.
questions.concept: Recognise this as 6 times the sum-of-squares formula.
calculation: Test small natural values of n in n(n+1)(2n+1).
Check 7: 6 / 7 is not whole. Fails. Check 12: 6 / 12 is not whole. Fails. Check 9: 6 / 9 is not whole. Fails.
Check 6: 6/6 = 1, 30/6 = 5, 84/6 = 14. All whole. Works.
Also, 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 is always a whole number, so n(n+1)(2n+1) is always a multiple of 6.
questions.info: This expression also contains 3 consecutive-ish structural factors (n, n+1, and the odd 2n+1) - recognising it from a known formula is far faster than testing many values.
questions.trick: If an expression resembles a standard summation formula's numerator (like sum of squares, cubes, etc), identify the formula first - the denominator of that formula is exactly the divisor you're looking for.

questions.q: For a statement P(n) to be true for all natural numbers n, which condition must be satisfied?
questions.given: Definition question - requirements of the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
questions.concept: Mathematical Induction requires: the base case P(1) is true, AND the inductive step P(k) implies P(k+1).
calculation: Principle of Mathematical Induction needs two things: (1) base case P(1) is true, and (2) if P(k) is true then P(k+1) is true.
Check each option against this.
Option A: P(k+1) = P(k) + 1 is not a rule of induction. Wrong.
Option B: P(k+2) = 2P(k) is not a rule of induction. Wrong.
Option D: P(k) + P(k+1) = P(k+2) is a Fibonacci-type relation, not induction. Wrong.
Option C: P(1) must be true. This is the base case, a required condition. Correct.
questions.info: Induction has TWO required parts (base case AND inductive step) - a statement is only proven for all n once BOTH parts are established, not just one.
questions.trick: Recall induction as a two-part checklist: (1) verify P(1), (2) assume P(k) and prove P(k+1) - any MCQ about 'what's needed' is testing recall of this exact pair.

questions.q: What is the inverse of the statement "if two lines are parallel, then they do not have any common point"?
options: If two lines are not parallel, then they have a common point
If two lines are parallel, then they have a common point
If two lines are not parallel, then they do not have a common point
If two lines are intersecting, then they do not have a common point
questions.given: Statement: 'if two lines are parallel, then they do not have any common point.'
questions.concept: The inverse of 'if P then Q' is 'if not-P then not-Q'.
calculation: Statement has the form: if p, then q.
p = 'two lines are parallel'. q = 'they do not have any common point'.
Inverse of 'if p then q' is 'if not p, then not q'. (Negate both parts, keep the order.)
not p = 'two lines are not parallel'.
not q = 'they have a common point' (negating 'do not have' gives 'have').
Inverse: If two lines are not parallel, then they have a common point.
Quick check of others: 'if p then not q' form is not inverse, and the converse swaps p and q. Only option A matches.
questions.info: Don't confuse inverse (not-P implies not-Q) with converse (Q implies P) or contrapositive (not-Q implies not-P) - all three are different, and only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.
questions.trick: Write out P and Q explicitly first, then just negate both and keep the same if-then direction - this mechanical substitution avoids logical mix-ups.

questions.q: p: Guava is a fruit. q: Rose is a flower. Which represents the conjunction?
options: Guava is not a fruit and rose is a flower
Guava is a fruit and rose is not a flower
Guava is a fruit and rose is a flower
Guava is a fruit or rose is a flower
questions.given: p: Guava is a fruit. q: Rose is a flower.
questions.concept: A conjunction joins two statements with AND, true only when BOTH parts are true.
calculation: Conjunction of p and q means 'p and q'. It is true only when both are true.
Disjunction means 'p or q'. Negation means 'not p'.
Option A: 'not p and q' has a negation. Wrong.
Option B: 'p and not q' has a negation. Wrong.
Option D: uses 'or', so it is a disjunction. Wrong.
Option C: 'Guava is a fruit and rose is a flower' is p and q. This is the conjunction.
questions.info: Contrast with disjunction (p OR q), which is true if EITHER part is true - conjunction is the stricter 'both must hold' combination.
questions.trick: Spot 'conjunction' = AND, 'disjunction' = OR instantly - then just join both original statements unchanged with that connector.
